canberra.title: Refusing to back down: CFMEU dumps litter collection duties in ACT pay dispute
canberra.snippet: Abandoned rubbish in Civic could just be the start of protected industrial action by CFMEU members as negotiations with the ACT Governmen...
canberra.content:
10 August 2026

Start the conversation

CFMEU union workers voted to stop collecting litter in Civic as part of protected industrial action. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Abandoned rubbish in Civic could just be the start of protected industrial action by CFMEU members as negotiations with the ACT Government drag on.

Members voted to ban the collection of litter (except where it posed an immediate health and safety risk, such as syringes and broken glass) both today (Monday, 10 August) and yesterday in protest over a year of bargaining.

CFMEU ACT Assistant Secretary Michael Hiscox said a sticking point was a proposed allowance for eligible employees who couldn’t work from home.

“[We’re after] a fair pay offer and the introduction of a frontline worker allowance that recognises the costs and pressure that comes with this work,” he said.

“The [current] offer doesn’t keep up with the cost of living.”

“GSOs [general service officers] take pride in keeping Canberra clean, safe, and maintained. They don’t take industrial action lightly, but have been left with no alternative in their fight for fair wages and proper recognition for the essential frontline work they perform.”

The $5800 yearly allowance demand has been described as recognition for the “additional costs, responsibilities and sacrifices” associated with performing essential work in person.

General service officers undertake work such as the maintenance of roads, paths, sports grounds and ACT Government buildings, as well as rubbish collection and mowing.

The union has also demanded a 5 per cent pay increase for workers this year, followed by a 4 per cent rise for 2027 and a 3 per cent rise for 2028 (the same increase backed by the CPSU).

Members have voted for an unlimited number of indefinite strikes and indefinite or periodic full and partial work bans.

This means the past two days may not be the last disruption for the Capital.

General service officers carry out work such as park and building maintenance, rubbish collection and mowing. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT Government has previously offered public servants a 3 per cent pay rise over three years.

City and Government Services Minister Tara Cheyne said the government had worked to minimise the impacts of the action as much as possible.

“It is very limited [action] to an area that has a higher number of people moving through it, and so it’s really quite visible,” she said.

“I really thank McDonald’s – there’s a very prominent bin outside McDonald’s [in Civic]; when I saw it yesterday [on Sunday] it was overflowing, and I appreciate that they are being good citizens about the surrounding public realm and taking responsibility for, ultimately, what is rubbish produced by their business.”

The Commonwealth Government put the CFMEU into administration in August 2024, but it is still operating under administration and representing members in bargaining negotiations.

An ACT Government spokesperson defended the latest offer as a “genuine effort to reach a fair and balanced agreement”.

“The offer would provide a pay rise above the projected rate of inflation for the next three years, along with substantial improvements in conditions,” they said.

“This builds on the Fair Go for GSOs outcome in the 2023-2026 Enterprise Agreement, which saw GSOs and other lower paid ACT public servants receive a significant pay increase.

“The offer recognises the important work of public servants while ensuring the long-term sustainability of the ACT’s finances.”

It’s understood a new offer will be put to ballot for the 11,000 staff covered by the Administrative Agreement in the coming weeks.

Bins in the Civic area will be prioritised for emptying and cleaning on Tuesday (11 August).

canberra.title: $2.12 at the bowser: Canberra motorists head to Queanbeyan for cheaper fuel
canberra.snippet: Canberra motorists are once again digging deeper at the bowser, with petrol prices climbing sharply after the Federal Government’s ...
canberra.content:
Fuel prices at Manuka Shell Station (10 August) if you have a fuel discount receipt: Photo: Naziya Alvi Rahman.

Canberra motorists are once again digging deeper at the bowser, with petrol prices climbing sharply after the Federal Government’s temporary fuel excise relief came to an end.

Regular unleaded averaged $2.12 a litre across the ACT on Monday (10 August), making Canberra the second most expensive capital city in the country behind Darwin, where motorists were paying an average of $2.17 a litre.

The surge has prompted many Canberrans to cross the border into Queanbeyan, where fuel prices were significantly cheaper.

Jenny, an ACT resident, said she drove to Queanbeyan after finding petrol selling for $1.89 a litre, compared with $2.09 at her local service station.

She was far from alone, with a steady stream of ACT-registered vehicles lining up to fill their tanks.

Fuel prices in Canberra have climbed dramatically from around $1.60 a litre in late June to today’s average, while premium 98 unleaded has risen above $2.38 at many service stations and diesel has exceeded $2.50 a litre.

According to the NRMA, the latest spike is largely the result of the Federal Government restoring fuel excise to its full rate, combined with ongoing instability in global oil markets.

The Commonwealth halved the fuel excise on 1 April, reducing it from 52 cents to 32 cents a litre to help offset higher fuel prices following tensions in the Middle East.

The relief began winding back on 1 July, when 16 cents a litre was reinstated, before ending completely on 3 August, returning the excise to its full indexed rate of 53.7 cents a litre.

An NRMA spokesperson said Canberra’s relatively small fuel market also contributed to higher prices.

“Prices have risen due to the removal of the fuel excise rebate combined with the ongoing US-Iran conflict,” the spokesperson said.

“Given current market conditions, falls in the order of five cents per litre are expected in the coming week. As with Darwin and Hobart, Canberra is a smaller market with less independent competition,” he told Region.

The ACT Government said it continues to work with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and consumer protection agencies across the country to monitor fuel pricing and ensure retailers are not unfairly increasing their margins.

“Fair Trading inspectors continue to monitor fuel pricing and are empowered to issue infringement notices where necessary to ensure prices paid by consumers at the bowser match advertised prices,” an ACT Government spokesperson said.

Earlier this year, the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Fuel Legislation Amendment Bill 2026, which gives the government new powers to collect information on fuel availability and strengthens consumer protections.

However, the government confirmed the legislation is not designed to influence retail fuel prices.

Instead, the new laws allow authorities to monitor fuel stocks and improve market oversight, while increasing penalties for service stations that charge motorists more than the advertised price.

“The increase related to the ending of the excise relief is unrelated to the amendments,” the spokesperson said.

Despite concerns from motorists about rising prices, the government said no fines have been issued under the legislation since it passed in May.

Officials said retailers had worked cooperatively to comply with the new fuel reporting requirements, with all ACT fuel retailers providing the required information since 1 July.

While Canberra drivers may receive some relief in the coming days, the NRMA says any decline is likely to be modest, with prices expected to fall by around five cents a litre if current market conditions continue.

canberra.title: ACT trails nation in bulk-billing growth rate
canberra.snippet: The bulk-billing rate has increased in the ACT since the Federal Government’s targeted investment in the scheme, but Canberra still...
canberra.content:
Bulk-billing rates have increased across the country, but growth has been the smallest in the ACT. Photo: Robyn Mac.

The bulk-billing rate has increased in the ACT since the Federal Government’s targeted investment in the scheme, but Canberra still lags behind the rest of the country.

Government figures just released show bulk-billing rates rose nationally in the June quarter, from 81.9 per cent to 84.1 per cent. Before Labor started its renewed investment in bulk-billing, the national rate had fallen to 75.6 per cent.

The biggest jump in the June quarter was in the Northern Territory, where its rates increased 13.0 percentage points to reach 90.8 per cent bulk-billing.

In the ACT, however, bulk-billing rates have increased by just 2.4 percentage points over the quarter to 59.3 per cent.

NSW was up 4.1 points to hit an 87.5 per cent rate; Victoria up 5.7 points to 85.7 per cent; Queensland increased 4,7 points to 82 per cent; South Australia up 6.0 points to 82.5 per cent; Tasmania’s rate grew 5.5 percentage points to 80.8 per cent; and Western Australia was up 4.8 points to 76.8 per cent.

The Federal Government committed $8.5 billion at the 2025 federal election to expand bulk-billing rates.

It has a stated goal of making 9 out of 10 GP visits free for patients by 2030.

The bulk billing rate for patients aged 16 to 64 years had the highest growth, increasing 8.2 percentage points to 78.6 per cent.

Federal Health Minister Mark Butler said there are now more than 3800 Medicare Bulk Billing Practices across Australia, with 1400 of those being mixed-billing practices before the government’s investments.

“Our government is delivering more bulk billing to more Australians,” he said.

“Across the country more and more GP practices are becoming fully bulk billing clinics, meaning all patients need is their Medicare card, not their credit card.

“It’s good for patients’ hip pockets and good for their health.”

The Minister said the almost five percentage point increase on the same quarter last year shows the bulk-billing rate nationally was continuing to increase “way ahead” of schedule.

Mr Butler also turned his attention to the government’s National Disability Insurance Scheme reforms, saying he wants them passed as soon as possible.

Getting them through the Senate this fortnight of parliament, the first sitting weeks after the mid-winter break, looked like it might be a big ask, as negotiations over the legislation grew increasingly contentious before the break and it was delayed for lack of support.

Talks have improved somewhat since then.

Anthony Albanese told the Labor Caucus on Monday (10 August) that he has spoken with Angus Taylor about reaching agreement on the reforms.

“I met earlier today with the Leader of the Opposition as well, to work through NDIS,” the Prime Minister said.

“I expect those changes will pass in this sitting fortnight, which will be important to make sure that it’s sustainable going forward.”

The government hopes the Coalition will help it to pass major changes to the NDIS, to reduce the scheme’s cost by more than $30 billion over four years.

Labor has put forward plans for sweeping changes to the scheme that narrow eligibility and accessibility, but also toughen regulation on providers to crack down on rorts and harm to participants.

A Senate inquiry into the draft legislation is also due to report back this week.

Mr Butler said he has had some constructive discussions with the Opposition over the planned reforms in the past few weeks and he remains hopeful that the standoff can be resolved before this sitting fortnight ends.

“We’re watching the Senate inquiry that’s still due to report later this week very closely, obviously, watching all of the evidence, and that includes the submissions made by the Human Rights Commission,” he said on Monday.

“At the moment, we are still convinced this is the right legislation to pass the parliament as soon as possible.

“I’d like to see it passed this fortnight because it is critical we start the work of getting the NDIS back on track.

“A lot of the reforms that I announced some months ago and are incorporated into this bill take effect over a period of time.

“We’ve had very constructive discussions, particularly with the Coalition. I’ll talk with them over the course of this week again, but I’ve been talking with Melissa McIntosh, really, since I made the announcement.

“She’s the shadow minister for the NDIS, obviously. And Angus Taylor has been very encouraging in his support, his recognition of the need to get the NDIS back on track and clarify some of those things that we’ve been talking about.

“Obviously, we’ve got further discussions to have over the course of this parliamentary sitting fortnight, but I take them at their word that they see this as something we can work together on.”

Before the break, Ms McIntosh had pushed for a three-day inquiry into the planned changes, but the Greens secured an eight-week extension and expressed their intention to vote the bill down.

Ms McIntosh has signalled a willingness to work with the government on amendments.

“This is a big reform to the NDIS. There’s no question that the expenditure is way out of control – $50 billion a year,” she said.

“But we need to get it right. The government needs to get it right.”

canberra.title: Letterbox drop ‘taking the piss’ on delivering strategic plan for Oaks Estate, MLAs claim
canberra.snippet: Community advocates and MLAs have slammed the ACT Government for using a letterbox drop to tick six actions off its strategic plan for Oa...
canberra.content:
Kurrajong MLAs Rebecca Vassarotti, Thomas Emerson and Elizabeth Lee want the ACT Government to do better when it comes to delivering for Oaks Estate residents. Photo: Supplied.

Community advocates and MLAs have slammed the ACT Government for using a letterbox drop to tick six actions off its strategic plan for Oaks Estate.

The unmarked envelopes contained pamphlets with information on how to report social housing maintenance and repair issues, responsible dog ownership, how to call the police, and how to submit Fix My Street reports.

Kurrajong MLAs Thomas Emerson (independent), Elizabeth Lee (Canberra Liberals) and Rebecca Vassarotti (ACT Greens) banded together to call out the lack of action to deliver real change for Oaks Estate residents.

“Sometimes it comes across like the development of the plan is the final product,” Mr Emerson said.

“But it’s about what happens on the ground, and doing a letterbox drop and saying that that ticks off six out of 37 actions in a strategic plan, frankly, is taking the piss.”

The ACT Government also wrote to taxi and rideshare companies asking them to increase their presence (or actually provide some service) to the border-hugging suburb.

Oaks Estate Residents Association president Fiona Macgregor said the community had such hope when consultation on the strategic action plan began.

“I think the government did a grand gesture, and I can’t fault the consultation,” she said.

“But when the plan came out, the community was totally disheartened.”

The Oaks Estate Strategic Plan contains 37 short-, medium- and long-term actions from 2025 to 2030 to make the suburb “safer, healthier and more connected”.

It’s a community without footpaths (bar one), shops or access to public transport.

The small suburb is home to multi-level public housing facilities, with the majority managed under head leases by charities, meaning the community is highly transient and vulnerable.

Mr Emerson said distributing information via letterboxes wasn’t appropriate.

“It’s not going to work where a lot of people are moving in and out of Oaks Estate each day, and that’s the source of some of the problems,” he said.

“One of the really simple asks from the Oaks Estate community is to have access to their own community hall. This is something that I understand the Deputy Chief Minister has promised to provide.

“Why wasn’t that done and prioritised ahead of dropping information in letterboxes, especially when residents have said this form of information provision isn’t actually what’s appropriate for their community?

“They need to be able to gather together in their town hall and share concerns and also hopefully actions coming out of this plan.”

Ms Macgregor said the government’s own research showed that giving people information about services didn’t increase their participation in them — but providing wraparound services where people lived did.

She also questioned why a pamphlet on how to contact the police was provided when submissions during the consultation pointed out that people feared retribution if they contacted the authorities and wanted CCTV installed to help them feel safe.

“What [we] wanted was community safety, public footpaths, a plan for public transport, and long-term answers on what’s going to happen with the public housing,” she said.

“Everybody has the right to live in a safe community, especially in Canberra.”

Health and Community Services Directorate director general Kareena Arthy told the recent budget estimates hearings that the letterbox drop wasn’t seen as “that’s it” in delivering for the area.

“It’s always very difficult to know how to get it right,” she said.

Ms Lee said the government needed to stop dragging its feet when it came to Canberra’s most vulnerable residents.

“It is time for the new Deputy Chief Minister [Rachel Stephen-Smith and Chief Minister Andrew Barr, who are both] local member[s] for Kurrajong to ensure that the most vulnerable people of our community, those ones that have no voice, are heard and taken seriously at the very, very top levels of this ACT government,” she said.

Ms Vassarotti agreed.

“One year into the strategic plan, there is an opportunity for the government to step up and actually show that they are committed to the implementation of the strategic plan, that they actually care and value the residents, and they are committed to ensuring that all members of the community get these basic municipal and community services,” she said.

The ACT Government is scheduled to provide a one-year update on the plan’s implementation during an upcoming sitting week.

Ms Lee said the results had better be good.

“It is going to be at the government’s peril if they ignore the concerns that have been raised by the Oaks Estate residents one year in.”

canberra.title: Griffith man to be sentenced after his winery altered invoices to claim millions in GST refunds
canberra.snippet: A former Griffith winemaker who pleaded guilty to three fraud offences after admitting his business altered supplier invoices to inflate ...
canberra.content:
10 August 2026

Aaron Salvestrin is due to be sentenced over fraud charges in November. Photo: First Choice Cellars/Facebook.

A former Griffith winemaker who pleaded guilty to three fraud offences after admitting his business altered supplier invoices to inflate the value of wine purchases and claim millions of dollars in GST refunds is due to be sentenced in November.

Aaron Salvestrin, 31, launched Sans Pareil Estate in Hanwood in 2018 and remained its owner and director until the company collapsed into liquidation four years later, with an alleged $32 million debt to the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).

Details of the winery’s spectacular rise and fall were first revealed by Region Riverina in an exclusive 2023 investigation.

Our reporting also exposed the scale of the business’s spending, including the purchase of a rare $1.47 million McLaren P1 supercar signed by Formula One driver Daniel Ricciardo.

According to a statement of facts tendered in the criminal case, Mr Salvestrin registered Sans Pareil as an export business and told the ATO he was selling large quantities of wine to a European buyer.

Businesses generally do not charge GST on goods exported overseas, meaning Sans Pareil could claim back GST it had supposedly paid when purchasing bulk wine from Australian suppliers for export.

The statement of facts says San Pareil used the system to claim millions of dollars in GST refunds to which it was not entitled.

In an interview with Australian Federal Police, Mr Salvestrin admitted that his business used PDF software to change genuine invoices from wine suppliers, increasing the value of the wine purchases shown on the documents.

The inflated invoices were then used to support GST refund claims.

The court heard Sans Pareil claimed more than $17 million in GST credits for purchases that did not occur.

The criminal case is against Mr Salvestrin alone, with no other Sans Pareil employees or former employees charged or accused of wrongdoing.

The ATO began auditing the business in June 2022, and the company went into liquidation in October that year.

The collapse triggered a separate civil case in the NSW Supreme Court, brought by the company’s liquidator, insolvency expert Gavin Moss, to recover money owed to both the ATO and other creditors — including Griffith and Wagga businesses.

In March 2024, Justice Anthony McGrath ordered Mr Salvestrin to repay more than $8.4 million after finding he had made “unreasonable director-related transactions” while running the business.

The civil case was separate from the criminal prosecution and did not result in criminal charges.

The liquidation also revealed the scale of the business’s spending, with funds allegedly used for expenses including luxury vehicles and other personal purchases. A McLaren P1 supercar signed by Formula One driver Daniel Ricciardo was sold for $1.47 million.

Aaron Salvestrin’s McLaren P1 Supercar was signed by Daniel Ricciardo. Photo: Orange_Kieth.

Mr Salvestrin declared himself bankrupt seven days after the Supreme Court ordered him to repay the $8.4 million.

The separate criminal investigation eventually resulted in Mr Salvestrin being charged with 16 counts of dishonestly intending to obtain a gain from a Commonwealth entity and one count of using a forged document to induce a public official to accept it as genuine.

He was granted bail in August 2025 and was required to report daily to Dee Why Police Station, surrender his passports and remain within the Sydney Northern Beaches area, where he currently lives. He was allowed to travel to Griffith with 24 hours’ notice to police.

The criminal case was delayed several times as lawyers worked through the large volume of evidence and negotiated on the charges.

In June this year, the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions withdrew the 16 charges of dishonestly intending to obtain a gain after Mr Salvestrin pleaded guilty to two charges of dishonestly intending to obtain a gain and one charge of using a forged document to induce a public official to accept it as genuine.

The remaining three offences were committed to the NSW District Court, where he is due to appear for sentencing on 26 November.

Mr Salvestrin will remain on bail until that date, under the same conditions imposed on him in August 2025.

The offences carry a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

australia.title: New head of Australian trade union movement named after Sally McManus steps down
australia.snippet: Melissa Donnelly, the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union, will replace the outgoing ACTU head Get our breaking n...
australia.content:
Melissa Donnelly, the national secretary of the Community and Public Sector Union, will take on the role as the next head of the trade movement in Australia, after the resignation of Sally McManus.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions’ secretary and its president, Michele O’Neil, revealed last month they would be stepping down after eight years together as the first all-female leadership team in the ACTU’s 99-year history, playing a major role in shaping the Albanese government’s workplace agenda.

On Monday, the ACTU executive met to elect 44-year-old Donnelly, who will be among the peak body’s youngest secretaries.

In a statement, Donnelly said it was a “tremendous honour” to take on the “important role”.

“Following in the footsteps of Sally is no easy task,” she said. “She has dedicated her life to fighting for fairer, safer and more secure workplaces.

“I am eager to get to work delivering real outcomes for working people and advancing the interests of workers across the country.

“Most of all, I am looking forward to meeting union members from every corner of Australia and serving alongside you as we work to lift living standards and secure a better future for all.”

Donnelly, who started her career as a lawyer in private practice, has led the CPSU for seven years, rising through the ranks after spearheading the union’s federal court case enabling public servants to participate in the nationwide “Your Rights at Work” campaign, which opposed the Howard government’s WorkChoices legislation.

In a statement, the CPSU said membership had grown by 23% during her tenure, with Donnelly pursuing flexible working arrangements, including a removal of caps on the number of days staff can work from home, delivering 18 weeks’ paid parental leave for both parents and leading the campaign to reverse the government outsourcing work to private consultancy firms.

Under her leadership, the CPSU has recently taken the tax office to the Fair Work Commission over alleged violations of the Albanese government’s “same job same pay” laws.

In a statement, the public service minister, Katy Gallagher, congratulated Donnelly and said the pair had worked “closely together” to rebuild “the public service and strengthened its capacity and capability to deliver for Australians”.

“Melissa has been a tireless advocate for public servants,” Gallagher said. “I know she’ll bring that same determination and experience to standing up for workers across Australia.”

McManus said Donnelly had “overwhelming support” across the union movement, describing her as “smart, strategic and completely focused on the needs of working people”.

“The average union member is a 44-year-old working mother and so is Melissa. She’s a year younger than I was when I took up the office and represents generational change,” she said.

“With two school-age children and having led a large union, she well knows the pressures working people are under. She has my full support, and I look forward to assisting her as she steps into the role.”

  • 14h ago

    Good morning

What we learned today, Monday 10 August

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for today.

Before we go, let’s take a look at what made the top headlines:

  • Peter Malinauskas, the South Australian premier, has announced a royal commission into artificial intelligence.

  • Prue Car, the NSW deputy premier, has asked the NSW Education Standards Authority to impose a ban on unsupervised take-home assessments during a broad review of AI’s impact on student learning.

  • Catherine King, the federal transport minister, met with Air Services Australia to about a “pathway forward” after two aircraft were involved in a near-miss at Sydney airport on Sunday.

  • Anthony Albanese has confirmed Labor will agree to amend its gambling legislation, promising action on inducements, as well as the targeting of advertising and how children may be exposed to ads.

  • The federal government is trumpeting “big benefits” from its Medicare investments, announcing bulk billing rates across the country are up nearly five percentage points since last year.

  • Police said what appeared to be a body found in a suitcase near Goulburn was not human – and was in fact a lifelike doll with markings resembling bruises and grazes.

  • Australia’s blind faith in the Aukus submarine deal is “stark staring bonkers”, the former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull has told a public inquiry, arguing the asymmetric deal with the US and UK will likely result in no submarines at all for Australia.

  • The Department of Defence has confirmed it is aware of reports that multiple drones were operating near RAAF Base Williamtown and Newcastle airport.

  • Sad news for music fans: Laneway festival is taking a “break” from Adelaide and Perth.

  • The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, has defended Anthony Albanese’s comments on a podcast after the former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami described them as “appalling” and “insulting”.

Thanks for joining us, see you bright and early tomorrow morning!

Jonathan Barrett

News Corp loses paid subscribers

News Corp’s stable of Australian newspapers has suffered a difficult 12 months, with four out of its five main mastheads losing paid subscribers, according to new company accounts.

Total paid subscribers for print and digital fell from 151,335 to 140,808 at the Daily Telegraph and 153,983 to 148,753 at the Herald Sun, according to analysis of annual figures.

Paid subscriber numbers also fell at the Courier Mail and the Advertiser.

The Rupert Murdoch-backed company did record an increase in paid subscribers at The Australian, rising from 335,903 to 341,975.

Last week, News Corp reported a slide across digital subscriptions at its Australian mastheads, erasing momentum gained in recent years.

The news division had been growing digital subscriptions in recent years amid a transition away from its reliance on a traditional newspaper base.

Andrew Hastie calls for federal parliamentary committee into AI instead of SA’s royal commission

The shadow industry minister, Andrew Hastie, has called for a federal parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence, rather than the South Australian royal commission announced today.

Hastie said he welcomed the SA premier Peter Malinauskas’ decision but believed the issue “sits within the realm of the national parliament”. Hastie said:

I do think artificial intelligence has strategic, moral and economic implications for the Australian people. And it’s really important that we look at this from a national perspective.

I think it should be a tripartisan committee that should examine the issues. Take as long as they need to ask the hard questions, take as many public submissions as possible, and see what comes of that.

‘Every tradie in Sydney has their wife as the director’: Icac witness questioned over fake invoices

Penry Buckley

Icac’s Operation Rosny has concluded hearings for today. Questioning of Jeremy Greenwood, who has been named in two of Icac’s allegations, focused on registered lobbying company Beckington, set up by Greenwood and Reformer Christian Ellis.

Beckington is alleged to have issued fake invoices for consulting advice for payments which in fact went to factional Liberal work.

Greenwood was asked about an arrangement under which Reformer Robert Assaf was paid a 10% finders fee for any new clients he brought to Beckington. The inquiry has previously heard that rather than being invoiced under Assaf’s name these were invoiced under Assaf’s wife name as being for education consultancy services.

Asked why Assaf had sought this arrangement, Greenwood said:

I just remember having a conversation and someone used the line, ‘Every tradie in Sydney has their wife as the director.’

Greenwood earlier told the commission that his wife was having contractions during the hearing today. There was no further update on this, and it is not known if it will have any impact on Greenwood’s expected appearance tomorrow.

‘Effectively double capacity soon’: Minns hopes second airport eases travel demand

New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, says he is cautiously optimistic about the opening of the state’s second airport, after days of chaos at Sydney airport.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Minns said Western Sydney international airport would increase the city’s aviation capacity when it opens to passengers in October.

We’ve got another airport opening soon, Western Sydney international airport, which will massively increase capacity in Sydney. I have to say, we are a little concerned if we are already stretched in our single airport or our major airport, because we are about to effectively double capacity soon.

The disruption has been attributed to air traffic controller staff shortages. Minns said the situation had highlighted the need to recruit and train more controllers at the new airport.

I didn’t realise it was a particular concern until this weekend when so many flights were cancelled and there were revelations about these two aircraft nearly colliding.

Obviously we will need to skill up and recruit a whole bunch of air traffic controllers to increase capacity in Sydney, which is going to be a huge boom for our economy and make life a lot easier for Sydney-based travellers.

Benita Kolovos

Victorian education minister puts forward revised teachers pay offer

The Victorian education minister, Gabrielle Williams, held a press conference this afternoon after putting a revised pay offer on the table to resolve the ongoing pay dispute with public school teachers.

The new offer builds on the previous offer of a 28.3% pay increase over four years by adding a $2,000 good faith payment for all teachers, enshrining workload management protections in the EBA and expanding a 1% increase for top of the range teachers to also cover education support staff.

She says its an “incredibly attractive offer” and would make the state’s teachers the “best paid” in the nation. Williams went on:

We of course hope that our teachers and education support staff will have a close look at this offer and understand that we come to this in a good place and wanting to genuinely ensure that we respect the incredibly important work they do in setting our children up for career pathways that are fulfilling and that ultimately also bolster our economy and our community. I just want to thank all of those teachers and education support staff for being along with us on this journey as we work together to try and get a fair deal. I know there is still a process to run, and we don’t want to preempt that process. It’s important that as a government we respect the process that now has to take place.

Members will vote on the new offer early next week. They had planned to strike on 19 August.

Krishani Dhanji

No imminent Labor conscience vote on telehealth for voluntary assisted dying

Labor MPs won’t get a conscience vote when the Greens and independent MP Kate Chaney introduce a bill to allow Australians to access voluntary assisted dying through telehealth services.

It’s despite Labor’s national conference in July deciding its members would get a conscience vote on the issue.

One MP used Monday’s meeting of the Labor caucus at Parliament House to ask the health minister, Mark Butler, how MPs would be able to vote on private member’s bills on the issue.

Butler told the caucus that procedural votes – for example, on whether a non-government bill should be progressed and brought forward for a vote – would be a binding party position.

Only when Labor introduces its own bill will the caucus be allowed to vote with their conscience. Butler said that move will not be imminent.

Penry Buckley

‘We have waited four years for this’: clashes over Icac witness’s memory of invoice

Returning to the Icac’s Operation Rosny, questioning of Jeremy Greenwood has focused on Catholic Schools NSW, which is under investigation for prohibited donations allegedly arranged and approved by CEO, Dallas McInerney, including through lobbying firm Beckington, set up by Reformer Christian Ellis and Greenwood in 2019.

Asked about proposals and a $16,000 invoice for work sent by Beckington to the schools governing body for work for July 2019, before the lobbying company was formally established, Greenwood repeatedly said he could not recall what work was done.

At one point, Dwyer asked: “Who can brief this commission, given your absence of memory, as to what work was actually done … ?”

Greenwood suggested asking Ellis, or former Catholic Schools NSW communications manager, James Tudehope, who is not named in Icac’s allegations but has declined a request to give evidence after moving to New Zealand this year. Ellis has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence.

After Greenwood said it was “inconvenient” for him that both men were overseas, Dwyer suggested it was “inconvenient for the commission … and inconvenient for the public trying to work out why this money was being committed on a monthly basis”.

Greenwood responds: “We have waited four years for this.”

‘Fork in the road’: SA royal commission to examine how AI is used in schools and government

Following our previous post on the announcement of a royal commission into AI in South Australia, the premier, Peter Malinauskas, said the inquiry would examine “how the technology is used and deployed in our society”.

The commission will look into how AI is implemented and deployed in workplaces, government services and other sectors. Malinauskas said:

I genuinely believe we are at a really important fork in the road where we can choose to allow this industry to come to our country and evolve in a way that is unregulated and unchecked, and we will be subject to the determinations it makes, rather than the other way around, or we can choose to set the agenda.

The commission will also focus on how young people use AI at school and across all levels of education. Malinauskas said:

Clearly we cannot afford a situation where a child comes out of school not knowing how to use AI. That would render them potentially redundant in a new modern labour market.

But simultaneously we can’t have children leaving school not knowing how to do calculations for themselves without AI and getting the balance right about how AI is used in schools and how it isn’t allowed to be used in schools.

SA premier announces royal commission into AI

South Australian premier Peter Malinauskas has announced a royal commission into artificial intelligence (AI).

Malinauskas has just come back from a trip to the US, where he met AI leaders and signed a memorandum of understanding with OpenAI.

At a press conference on Monday, Malinauskas said the commission would examine the future impacts of AI and place South Australia at the forefront of the global debate about its use. He said the royal commission would start in October, report no later than 1 July 2027, and would look at the impacts, risks and opportunities of AI across education, industry, public health, arts and culture. He said AI’s rapid development could not occur “unchecked”.

The Labor government I lead has a record of stepping up and protecting young people when it comes to social media, and this is no different.

We are looking to embrace the opportunity of AI, but not in a way that leaves us with regrets.

He said the discussion should focus on “how it will be deployed in our society, which is far more consequential than where a datacentre gets built”. He said:

Never before in human history have we contended with a world where there is something that’s smarter than us. Now we have it, and its intelligence is only going to increase at warp speed over the course of the next two years alone. That will change everything, and we need to make sure that what it changes is done on our terms for the interests of people.

Albanese confirms amendments to gambling laws, including inducements and ads

Josh Butler

Prime minister Anthony Albanese has confirmed Labor will agree to amend its gambling legislation, promising action on inducements, as well as the targeting of advertising and how children may be exposed to ads.

We’re still chasing the particular details of what the government is onboard with, after a meeting between Albanese and Angus Taylor which the Liberals described as “very positive”.

Albanese told his caucus that “further work and amendments” would be coming on gambling inducements, including “making sure that those issues are dealt with in a constructive way, making sure that we get the balance right between people who want to go along and have a punt on a Saturday at the races, but also that problem gambling is actually dealt with.”

Albanese didn’t provide specifics, but he said the legislation would be amended in the House of Representatives this week to include “some really practical amendments dealing with the targeting of advertising, dealing with reducing children’s exposure”.

More to come soon.

australia.title: Victorian Liberals promise weekly red bin garbage collections for all, calling fortnightly system ‘disgusting’
australia.snippet: If opposition wins November’s state election, leader Jess Wilson vows households will not pay more under the change Follow our Australia ...
australia.content:
The Victorian Liberals have vowed to restore weekly rubbish collections if they win November’s state election, with leader Jess Wilson describing the current fortnightly system in her local area as “disgusting”.

Thirty-three Victorian councils have switched general rubbish collections from weekly to fortnightly, with a similar shift occurring in other states.

In metropolitan Melbourne they include Banyule, Bayside, Boroondara, Glen Eira, Knox, Manningham, Monash, Nillumbik and Yarra Ranges.

Merri-bek is also expected to follow from mid-2027, in a move it has said would save ratepayers $16m over 10 years, help keep food waste out of landfill and reduce pollution.

Under Merri-bek’s proposal, the standard red-lid rubbish bin would increase from 80 litres to 120 litres, while certain households, such as those with multiple children in nappies, could get bigger bins for free.

But Wilson said if elected in November, a Liberal-National government would require councils to collect general rubbish every week.

She said her government would also apply the council rate cap – which now limits annual rate increases to inflation – to waste charges, so households would not pay more as a result of the change.

The opposition leader, whose electorate of Kew falls within the Boroondara local government area, said reverting to weekly general rubbish collections was “common sense”.

“To be perfectly honest – it’s disgusting. The bins are overflowing. I have a toddler, we have nappies and we have many little kids on our street with large families,” Wilson told 3AW radio on Monday.

“You know what it’s like on bin night, when you have two or three extra bags and you’re trying to find somewhere to put them. They end up in council parks in the bins there overflowing.”

In a statement, she added that weekly rubbish collection was an “essential service that shouldn’t depend on your postcode”.

Wes Gault, the mayor of Boroondara, said he agreed that residents were “paying too much for waste disposal”, but it was due to the state government’s landfill levy, which has increased significantly in recent years.

“[This change] will cost our residents at least $3m more a year in trucks, fuel, servicing and staffing alone – not including the extra landfill levies,” Gault said in a statement.

He also said that 70% of material collected across all Boroondara’s kerbside bins was diverted from landfill.

“Bringing back a weekly landfill collection risks undermining that progress, [via] increasing emissions through more truck collections and potent landfill methane.”

The council said residents can also upsize to 120 or 240-litre bins at an additional cost if they had increased volumes of nappies.

Most councils that have switched to fortnightly collection have cited the introduction of weekly food organics and garden organics (Fogo) collection as the main reason for the change.

They have said the shift encourages residents to place food scraps in a green bin, which can then be turned into compost rather than sent to landfill, where they break down and produce methane.

Whitehorse council has considered making the change but decided to keep weekly collection. In material sent to residents as part of its consultation, the council said food waste was accounting for 40% of the weight of rubbish bins.

It said Boroondara, Knox, Manningham and Monash had “reduced the amount of waste sent to landfill by an average of 19%” in the first year after switching to weekly Fogo collections and fortnightly general rubbish collections.

It is not the first time rubbish has made headlines this year, with several Victorian councils in April pushing back against a mandated deadline to introduce a fourth, purple-lidded bin for glass by 1 July 2027 as part of a shift to a statewide four-bin system.

The government first announced the overhaul of the state’s rubbish collection in 2020, following the collapse of the state’s largest recycling company SKM a year earlier, which resulted in thousands of tonnes of recycling being sent to landfill.

The Liberals have committed to reviewing the landfill levy, if elected, as well as make the purple bin option.

In Western Australia, the One Nation candidate Luke Herdegen is using a state byelection to campaign for Rockingham council to restore weekly rubbish collection.

australia.title: Two workers temporarily stood down after near-miss collision at Sydney airport
australia.snippet: Transport minister says improved staff rostering will be in place from next month after ‘unacceptable’ delays and incident involving Qata...
australia.content:
The transport minister, Catherine King, has said improved staff rostering will be in place at Sydney airport from next month after “unacceptable” delays and a near-miss collision that resulted in two workers being stood down.

King called in the Airservices Australia chief executive officer, Rob Sharp, for a meeting in Canberra on Monday, the day after a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided hitting a Qatar Airways plane that was pulled across the runway in front of it.

Two staff involved in the incident – an Airservices Australia air traffic controller and the tug driver who was towing the Qatar plane – were stood down while they completed standard post-incident drug and alcohol testing.

The temporary loss of an air traffic controller only exacerbated delays at Australia’s biggest airport, where staff shortages had already resulted in days of disruption.

Additionally, a cabin crew member onboard the Jetstar plane was injured when the planes stopped abruptly, and some equipment was damaged.

The incident occurred less than two weeks after another near-miss relating to air traffic control on the tarmac at Sydney. On 27 July, a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of one of the airline’s other planes that had just landed.

King on Monday said the delays and disruptions were unacceptable, but she was “confident” that Airservices Australia was “doing everything they can to get on top of this”.

“Airservices have committed to implementing improved rostering practices for Sydney’s Air Traffic Controllers that will be implemented from early September,” she said.

King said the situation would be “carefully” managed for the rest of August.

A new Sydney Tower simulator had also been installed to increase training capacity and enable more air traffic controllers to be trained, she said.

“It has been a big focus of ours to encourage more people to enter the profession, and 95 people are expected to be endorsed as air traffic controllers by the end of the year,” King said.

“Six controllers are currently training in Sydney Tower, with another 15 expected to commence before the end of 2027.”

King said she wanted to “give a shout out” to the air traffic controllers, who
are dealing with “a really stressful and difficult job” and “did a very good job over the weekend to try to manage the disruptions as best they could”.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) is investigating both the Sunday incident and the 27 July near-miss involving Qantas aircraft.

The head of the ATSB, Angus Mitchell, on Monday said the two incidents were unacceptable.

“Planes should not be getting that close and we should never have to rely on, as has happened in both these instances, pilots at the last minute, making an emergency decision to prevent them coming together,” he told ABC radio.

Investigators would interview flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses, and review any CCTV footage, the ATSB said.

A source told Guardian Australia on Sunday that initial inquiries suggested the tug vehicle pulling the Qatar aircraft may not have followed instructions.

The tug driver was believed to work for Menzies Aviation, a UK-headquartered third party contractor that provides ground staff for Qatar Airways at Sydney airport.

A Menzies Aviation spokesperson said in a statement that it had launched a thorough investigation into the incident and was fully cooperating with the ATSB.

“We are sorry to hear that a member of the cabin crew was injured and recognise that incidents of this nature can be concerning,” the statement said.

“The safety of our people, customers and the travelling public is our highest priority. We will carefully review the findings of both investigations to ensure any lessons identified are fully addressed.”

Michael Kaine, the national secretary of the Transport Workers’ Union, which represents air traffic controllers and airport ground crews, said the aviation industry was in “crisis” due to staff shortages and poor conditions.

“Across the industry, this revolving-door workforce is understaffed and exhausted,” he said.

“We’ve seen another worker hurt from this incident after a horrific string of injuries and a worker killed at Qantas Freight last year.”

Qatar Airways was contacted for comment.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Sydney airport chaos; ‘body’ in suitcase actually lifelike doll; and a breakfast of champions
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon. Sydney airport was in chaos over the weekend. On Saturday, more than 150 flights were delayed, and then on Sunday, two planes, owned by Jetstar and Qatar Airways, almost collided.

The political fallout began on Monday, when Catherine King, the federal transport minister, called in the Airservices Australia chief executive officer, Rob Sharp, for a meeting in Canberra. Two staff involved in the incident – an Airservices Australia air traffic controller and the tug driver who was towing the Qatar plane – were stood down while they completed standard post-incident drug and alcohol testing.

King has said improved staff rostering will be in place at Sydney airport from next month after the near miss and the “unacceptable” delays over the weekend.

What they said …

“We are still undertaking more forensic work to identify what they are. But we can identify that they’re not human.” – Supt Linda Bradbury

What appeared to be a woman’s body found in a suitcase by the side of a road near Goulburn in regional New South Wales was not in fact human remains, police say. NSW police were called to Wolgon Road in Oallen about 12.50pm on Sunday “following reports a body had been located”. world.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
world.snippet: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce tempora...
world.content:
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

world.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
world.snippet: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians Temporary protected status...
world.content:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

Meanwhile, in a statement on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. People ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
world.snippet: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation The virus causing a ma...
world.content:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

world.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
world.snippet: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon The US state department is to shu...
world.content:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

world.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
world.snippet: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone The Ugandan football comm...
world.content:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”
